lines.text: Here's why. The robot tracks where it is mostly by counting wheel turns. That's called odometry.
Each wheel turn rolls out about thirty-five centimeters of carpet. Add up the turns, and you know how far you went.
But a slipping wheel turns without moving the robot. The count grows anyway, so the robot thinks it's somewhere it isn't.
In our simulator, a one-loop command jump over-counted by up to one and a half meters. Even careful hard driving cost up to thirty-five centimeters.
Now remember the job: stop on a scoring spot within two centimeters.
Close to the target, the camera can lose sight of the tag. Then the robot finishes on odometry alone.
If odometry is wrong, the robot parks in the wrong place, and thinks it's right.
So we want the robot to push as hard as it can, but never harder than its tires can grip.
